name: Cucumber
description: The universal cooling salad vegetable.

name: Tomato
description: The base of half the world's gravies and salads.

ayurveda.note: Sour-pungent; classically pitta-aggravating.

histamine.note: One of the biggest everyday histamine offenders.

name: Spinach
description: Soft leafy green cooked across all four cuisines.

histamine.note: Surprisingly high histamine for a 'healthy' green.

name: Lettuce
description: Crisp salad leaf; khass is a classic Unani cooler.

unani.note: Khass appears in classical cooling prescriptions.

name: Cabbage
description: Dense leafy head, raw or cooked.

histamine.note: Fresh cabbage is safe — fermented (sauerkraut/kimchi) is a 3.

name: Napa cabbage
description: Sweet crinkly cabbage of Chinese soups and stir-fries.

ayurveda.note: Not classical; inferred from cabbage family.

histamine.note: Fresh is safe; kimchi form is a 3.

name: Bok choy
description: Crunchy-stemmed Chinese green.

ayurveda.note: Not classical; inferred.

name: Cauliflower
description: White brassica head; aloo gobi's other half.

ayurveda.note: Cooling but gas-forming (vata).

name: Broccoli
description: Green brassica florets.

name: Carrot
description: Sweet root; salad, sabzi, and gajar halwa.

ayurveda.note: Mildly heating; cooked more so.

unani.note: Gajar leans garam in desi usage — hence a winter halwa.

name: Potato
description: The universal starchy staple.

histamine.note: Safe staple (freshly cooked; not leftover fried).

name: Sweet potato
description: Sweet orange root, roasted street-side in winter.

ayurveda.note: Sweet-heavy = cooling per some; others call it warming.

unani.note: Sold as a winter warming food in desi bazaars.

name: Onion
description: The base of nearly every gravy on earth.

histamine.note: Well tolerated; raw excess bothers some stomachs (not histamine).

name: Okra
description: Green pods beloved as bhindi and bamia stew.

tcm.note: Thin classical documentation.

name: Eggplant
description: Glossy purple nightshade; bharta, moussaka, yu xiang qie zi.

tcm.note: TCM calls it cooling — the exact opposite of the desi view.

unani.note: Baingan is famously garam and 'badi' in desi usage.

name: Bitter gourd
description: Intensely bitter pod, prized medicinally in two traditions.

tcm.note: The definitive heat-clearing vegetable.

name: Bottle gourd
description: Pale watery gourd; the desi sickbed vegetable.

ayurveda.note: The classic cooling sabzi.

name: Ridge gourd
description: Ridged soft gourd cooked as a light sabzi.

name: Zucchini
description: Tender summer squash; kousa mahshi's shell.

name: Pumpkin
description: Sweet orange squash.

tcm.note: TCM calls nan gua warming — unlike the gourds it resembles.

unani.note: Kaddu is thanda in desi usage — disagrees with TCM.

name: Winter melon / ash gourd
description: Huge pale gourd; TCM's summer-heat soup and Agra's petha sweet.

tcm.note: The classic summer heat-clearing soup gourd.

name: Radish / daikon
description: Peppery crisp root, from salad mooli to braised daikon.

tcm.note: Raw cool; cooked closer to neutral.

ayurveda.note: Pungent = heating classically — disagrees with folk 'mooli thandi'.

unani.note: Desi folk call mooli thandi; some hakims call it hot-dry.

name: Turnip
description: Winter root; shalgam sabzi and Arabic pickled lift.

unani.note: Shaljam is a classic winter garam vegetable.

histamine.note: Fresh fine; pickled lift is fermented — avoid when reactive.

name: Beetroot
description: Earthy crimson root.

unani.note: Chukandar leans garam; given for blood-building.

name: Bell pepper / capsicum
description: Sweet non-spicy pepper.

ayurveda.note: Milder than chili but still pungent-family.

histamine.note: Sweet peppers are fine — unlike hot chilies.

name: Mushroom (button)
description: Everyday white mushroom.

ayurveda.note: Classically discouraged (tamasic) more than classified.

histamine.note: Fungi accumulate amines as they age — eat very fresh.

name: Shiitake mushroom
description: Meaty aromatic mushroom, fresh or dried.

ayurveda.note: Not classical; inferred.

histamine.note: Dried/aged forms carry more amines than fresh.

name: Green beans
description: Tender pod beans.

name: Green peas
description: Sweet green pulse of matar paneer and fried rice.

name: Corn
description: Sweet kernels, roasted bhutta to congee.

ayurveda.note: Drying and mildly heating.

unani.note: Makai (and its roti) is a winter garam food.

name: Celery
description: Crunchy watery stalk.

tcm.note: Used for liver-heat and blood pressure in TCM.

histamine.note: Histamine-safe, but a true allergen for a minority (celery allergy).

name: Asparagus
description: Tender green spears.

unani.note: Halyoon is hot in classical Unani — disagrees with TCM/Ayurveda.

name: Kale
description: Sturdy dark leafy green.

ayurveda.note: Cooling but drying/roughening (vata).

name: Mustard greens
description: Pungent winter green of sarson-da-saag and Chinese pickles.

histamine.note: Fresh fine; Chinese pickled gai choy is fermented — avoid when reactive.

name: Fenugreek leaves
description: Bitter aromatic leaf of methi parathas and aloo methi.

name: Taro
description: Starchy nutty corm; arbi sabzi and Egyptian qolqas.

ayurveda.note: Heavy and kapha-forming; classifications vary.

unani.note: Arbi is often called thandi and 'badi' (gas-forming).

name: Lotus root
description: Crunchy perforated rhizome of soups and stir-fries.

tcm.note: Raw is cold (clears heat); cooked becomes neutral-warm and tonifying.

name: Water spinach
description: Hollow-stemmed green, flash-fried with garlic.

ayurveda.note: Not classical; inferred.

name: Snow peas
description: Flat edible-pod peas.

name: Spring onion
description: Mild green onion; TCM's cold-expelling cong bai.

tcm.note: The white part is a classic cold-and-flu warming herb.

name: Tinda / apple gourd
description: Small round pale gourd of Punjabi summer cooking.

tcm.note: Not classical; inferred from gourd family.

histamine.note: Sparse data; gourds are reliably safe.

name: Drumstick
description: Long ridged pod simmered into sambar — you chew the pulp and drop the fibre.

tcm.note: No classical Chinese entry; placed from its pungent, warming character.

ayurveda.note: Shigru is ushna and tikshna — a classic kapha- and vata-reducing vegetable.

unani.note: Sahjan is garam-khushk, used against swelling and cold complaints.

histamine.note: Low; a cooked pod, nothing fermented.

name: Ivy gourd
description: Thumb-sized gourd sliced and fried dry — the weekday sabzi.

tcm.note: Not classically listed; read with the gourd family, which is cooling.

ayurveda.note: Bimbi is shita and light; long used in the diabetic diet.

histamine.note: Fresh gourd; among the safest vegetables.

name: Pointed gourd
description: Small striped gourd, light enough to be fed to the recovering.

tcm.note: Outside the Chinese record; grouped with the cooling gourds.

ayurveda.note: Patola is classically shita, laghu (light) and deepana — named in texts as suitable during fever.

name: Snake gourd
description: Long coiling gourd with mild white flesh, cooked soft.

tcm.note: Related species appear in the Chinese record as cooling.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light, in the patola group.

name: Cluster beans
description: Slightly bitter flat beans, stir-fried with plenty of spice.

tcm.note: No classical entry.

ayurveda.note: Astringent and kapha-reducing; read as shita, though heavy to digest.

unani.note: Thanda and drying, from its astringency.

name: Flat beans
description: Broad flat pods — must be cooked right through, never eaten raw.

tcm.note: Bai bian dou is slightly warm and a standard spleen tonic for damp conditions.

ayurveda.note: Nishpava is described as ushna and vata-provoking — heavy on the gut.

unani.note: Garam and windy in desi usage.

histamine.note: Low. Raw or undercooked pods are toxic — a lectin problem, not a histamine one.

name: Elephant yam
description: Huge starchy tuber, itchy raw and eaten at Diwali.

tcm.note: Not the Chinese shan yao; placed from its pungent, drying character.

ayurveda.note: Surana is ushna, tikshna and kapha-reducing — the classical remedy for arshas (piles).

unani.note: Garam-khushk, which is why it is cooked with tamarind to cut it.

histamine.note: Low for histamine; the raw itch is calcium oxalate, a different mechanism.

name: Colocasia leaves
description: Big heart-shaped leaves smeared with besan, rolled and steamed.

tcm.note: No classical entry for the leaf.

ayurveda.note: Shita and astringent, though heavy — always cooked with souring agents.

unani.note: Thanda; the raw leaf is an irritant.

histamine.note: Low; the raw scratch is oxalate, which tamarind or lemon in the recipe neutralises.

name: Amaranth greens
description: Soft red-veined summer greens that wilt down to almost nothing.

tcm.note: Xian cai clears heat and is eaten through the hot months.

ayurveda.note: Tanduliya is classically shita and pitta-pacifying — a summer saag.

histamine.note: Not on the SIGHI list. Spinach is the leafy green singled out there; amaranth is generally easier.

name: Bathua
description: Winter weed-green, cooked into saag or stirred through raita.

tcm.note: Not classically listed.

ayurveda.note: Vastuka is shita, light and mildly laxative.

unani.note: Thanda, taken to cool the blood.

histamine.note: Low, though it is oxalate-rich like spinach.

name: Kachnar
description: Unopened flower buds cooked as a sabzi in early spring.

tcm.note: No Chinese entry.

ayurveda.note: Kanchanara is shita and kashaya, the classical drug for glandular swellings.

unani.note: Thanda and astringent in regional usage.

name: Green papaya
description: Unripe papaya shredded into salads or cooked as a vegetable.

tcm.note: The unripe fruit is not separately classified; read from its enzyme-rich, stimulating character.

ayurveda.note: Unripe papaya is strongly ushna and emmenagogue — the reason it is traditionally avoided in pregnancy.

unani.note: Garam, and used to bring on delayed courses.

histamine.note: Papain is at its strongest in the unripe fruit — the same liberator flag as ripe papaya, more so.

name: Banana flower
description: Purple bud chopped fine and soaked — astringent, faintly bitter.

tcm.note: No classical entry.

ayurveda.note: Shita and kashaya; long used for excessive bleeding.

histamine.note: Low; it discolours fast, so it is soaked in acidulated water.

name: Bamboo shoots
description: Pale crisp shoots, sliced into stir-fries and hotpot.

tcm.note: Zhu sun is cold — it clears heat and resolves phlegm, and is held back from cold constitutions.

ayurveda.note: Not classical outside the northeast; read as shita.

histamine.note: Fresh and canned are low; the pickled and fermented kinds are a different matter entirely.

name: Wood ear mushroom
description: Crunchy black fungus with almost no flavour of its own.

tcm.note: Hei mu er is neutral, cools the blood and is taken to keep the vessels moving.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

histamine.note: Low dried and rehydrated. Soaking it warm for hours is a food-safety problem, not a histamine one.

name: White fungus
description: Ruffled translucent fungus simmered with rock sugar into a sweet soup.

tcm.note: Yin er is a neutral yin tonic that moistens the lung — the classic autumn-dryness dessert.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry; read from its moistening use.

name: Enoki mushroom
description: Long thin white stems in a clump — a hotpot standard.

tcm.note: Read as cool and heat-clearing, like most cultivated mushrooms.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

histamine.note: Low fresh. Mushrooms climb quickly once they start to age.

name: Oyster mushroom
description: Fan-shaped and meaty — the mushroom that stands in for chicken.

tcm.note: Ping gu is neutral and mildly tonifying.

ayurveda.note: Mushrooms sit awkwardly in the classical texts, which are wary of them.

histamine.note: Low fresh; ageing mushrooms rise fast.

nutrition.highlight: meaty enough to stand in for chicken

name: Nori
description: Paper-thin roasted seaweed sheets, wrapped or crumbled into soup.

tcm.note: Zi cai is cold and softens hardness — the seaweeds are a cooling group in TCM.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

histamine.note: Dried and aged sea products carry histamine; seaweed is a known trigger for the sensitive.

name: Kelp
description: Thick dried sea ribbons, simmered for stock or eaten in salads.

tcm.note: Kun bu is cold and the classical drug for goitre and lumps — softens what is hard.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

histamine.note: Like other dried sea products, it can be a trigger. Iodine load is its own separate caution.

name: Water chestnut
description: Crisp white corm that stays crunchy however long you cook it.

tcm.note: Ma ti is cold, clears heat and generates fluids — eaten raw in summer.

ayurveda.note: Shringataka is shita; singhare ka atta is a standard fasting flour.

name: Burdock root
description: Long earthy root, scrubbed and braised or shredded into stir-fries.

tcm.note: The burdock family is cooling and detoxifying; niu bang zi, the seed, is a standard heat-clearing drug.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

name: Garlic chives
description: Flat green blades with a garlic bite, folded into dumplings and eggs.

tcm.note: Jiu cai is warm and yang-tonifying — explicitly a winter and kidney-warming vegetable.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry; the allium character reads ushna.

unani.note: Garam like the rest of the onion family.

name: Chayote
description: Pale green squash with mild flesh — cooks fast, tastes of what it's cooked with.

tcm.note: A new-world squash; grouped with the cooling gourds.

ayurveda.note: Read with the shita gourd family; light and easily digested.

name: Jicama
description: Crisp sweet root eaten raw in sticks, like a juicier apple.

tcm.note: Sha ge is cool and generates fluids, eaten raw against summer thirst.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

name: Brussels sprouts
description: Miniature cabbages — bitter boiled, sweet roasted.

tcm.note: Read with cabbage, which is neutral in the Chinese record.

ayurveda.note: Grouped with the cabbage family — shita but wind-forming.

name: Leek
description: Mild sweet allium, sweated down as the base of soups.

tcm.note: The cong family is warm and disperses cold — the classic first-sign-of-a-chill vegetable.

ayurveda.note: Ushna like the rest of the onion family, if gentler.

unani.note: Kurrath is garam-khushk in the Unani record.

name: Fennel bulb
description: Crisp aniseed bulb, shaved raw into salad or roasted to sweetness.

tcm.note: Xiao hui xiang is warm and disperses cold from the lower abdomen — the same reading as the seed.

ayurveda.note: Follows saunf: classically shita and pitta-pacifying, which is why it is chewed after meals.

unani.note: Thanda in desi usage, taken against acidity and heat — the exact opposite of the Chinese reading.

histamine.note: Very low; among the safest vegetables on the list.

name: Artichoke
description: Thistle bud eaten leaf by leaf, down to the heart.

tcm.note: Not part of the Chinese record.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry; bitter and read as shita.

unani.note: Kharshuf appears in the Arab record as a bitter liver-cooling vegetable.

name: Swiss chard
description: Big glossy leaves on coloured stems — spinach's sturdier cousin.

tcm.note: Read with the cooling leafy greens.

ayurveda.note: Shita, in the leafy-green group.

unani.note: Saluq is thanda in the Arab record, cooked with lemon and garlic.

histamine.note: Grouped with spinach, which SIGHI rates poorly — the same oxalate-rich leafy family.

name: Arugula
description: Peppery leaf served in bunches on the mezze table.

tcm.note: No Chinese entry; the mustard-family pungency reads warm.

ayurveda.note: Katu (pungent) and read as ushna.

unani.note: Jarjeer is documented as garam-khushk and reputed as an aphrodisiac.

name: Watercress
description: Small peppery leaves that grow in running water — a Cantonese soup green.

tcm.note: Xi yang cai clears lung heat and moistens dryness — simmered into long autumn soups.

ayurveda.note: Pungent mustard-family leaf, read as ushna.

unani.note: The cress family is garam in Unani, used to disperse cold and phlegm — the reverse of the Chinese reading.

name: Endive
description: Tight pale bitter leaves, eaten raw as scoops or braised soft.

tcm.note: Not classically listed; bitter greens are read as cooling.

ayurveda.note: Tikta (bitter) rasa is shita and pitta-clearing.

unani.note: Hindiba is one of the best-documented cooling drugs in Unani — a standard liver and blood cooler.

name: Baby corn
description: Whole tiny cobs picked before the kernels set — eaten stalk and all.

tcm.note: Read with mature corn, which is neutral.

ayurveda.note: The immature cob is lighter and moister than the mature grain.

unani.note: Placed by analogy to young, watery vegetables.

histamine.note: Low fresh; the tinned kind sits in brine, which is a separate question.

name: Lotus seeds
description: Puffed white seeds — roasted as a snack, or simmered into kheer and soup.

tcm.note: Lian zi is neutral, tonifies the spleen and kidney and calms the shen — it suits hot and cold constitutions alike.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light — which is why makhana is a fasting-day food.

unani.note: Thanda, taken as a strengthening food.

histamine.note: Very low — one of the safest snacks on a reactive day.

name: Green garlic
description: Young garlic pulled before the bulb splits — milder, greener, seasonal.

tcm.note: The allium group is warm and disperses cold; young garlic is gentler than the cured bulb.

ayurveda.note: Lashuna is ushna and tikshna — heating whatever its age.

unani.note: Garam-khushk, a winter vegetable in the desi kitchen.

name: Bean sprouts
description: Sprouted mung beans — crisp, watery, thrown in at the last second.

tcm.note: Dou ya clears heat and drains damp, like the mung bean it comes from.

ayurveda.note: Sprouting lightens an already shita bean.

unani.note: Thanda-tar; moong is the coolest of the dals.

histamine.note: Low, but sprouts spoil quickly and are a food-safety risk when old — a different problem from histamine.

name: Choy sum
description: Slim flowering stems with small yellow buds — blanched and dressed in oyster sauce.

tcm.note: Read with the brassica greens, which clear heat gently.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry; grouped with leafy greens.

name: Shallots
description: Small copper-skinned onions — sweeter, sharper and far more aromatic than the big kind.

tcm.note: The cong family is warm and disperses cold; shallot is used the same way as spring onion.

ayurveda.note: Palandu is ushna and tikshna, like all the alliums.

unani.note: Garam-khushk; the sambar onion of South Indian cooking.

histamine.note: Low fresh; fried crisp shallots keep badly and go rancid, which is a separate problem.

name: Cassava
description: Starchy tuber that must be cooked properly — raw or under-cooked it is genuinely toxic.

tcm.note: A new-world root; read with the starchy tubers.

ayurveda.note: Shita and very guru — heavy, filling and slow.

unani.note: Thanda-tar; the Kerala staple eaten with fish curry.

histamine.note: Low for histamine. Its real hazard is cyanogenic glycosides in raw or badly processed root — a different mechanism entirely.

name: Kohlrabi
description: A swollen stem that grows above ground — crisp and mild, like a sweet broccoli stalk.

tcm.note: Read with the brassicas, which are neutral to cool.

ayurveda.note: Shita and wind-forming, like the cabbage family.

unani.note: Thanda-khushk; cooked with hing for exactly that reason.

name: Purslane
description: Succulent sour-tasting weed-green, eaten in salads and cooked as saag.

tcm.note: Ma chi xian is cold and clears heat and toxin — a classical drug for dysentery.

ayurveda.note: Shita and sour; a summer green.

unani.note: Baqle is barid-ratab in Unani and a standard cooling green.

histamine.note: Low, though it is oxalate-rich like spinach.

name: Gai lan
description: Thick blue-green stems with small flowers — blanched and dressed, faintly bitter.

tcm.note: A brassica; cool and heat-clearing, with the bitter edge that marks it.

ayurveda.note: Tikta and shita.

name: Moringa leaves
description: The leaves of the drumstick tree — cooked as saag, or dried into powder.

tcm.note: Read with the drumstick pod; pungent and warming.

ayurveda.note: Shigru patra is ushna, tikshna and kapha-reducing, like the pod.

unani.note: Garam-khushk; used against swelling and cold conditions.

name: Horseradish
description: Fiercely pungent root grated raw — the heat goes up the nose, not down the throat.

tcm.note: The mustard-family pungency is hot and strongly dispersing.

ayurveda.note: Katu and ushna in a high degree.

unani.note: Garam-khushk; a classical drug for cold phlegm.

histamine.note: Low, though the pungency irritates independently of histamine.

nutrition.highlight: the heat goes up, not down

name: Parsnip
description: Pale sweet root that turns sweeter after frost — roasted more often than boiled.

tcm.note: Read with carrot, sweeter and starchier.

ayurveda.note: Madhura and read as gently ushna; no classical entry.

name: Celeriac
description: The knobbly root of a celery relative — nutty, and better mashed than boiled.

tcm.note: Read with celery, which is cool and calms the liver.

ayurveda.note: Follows celery; no separate classical entry.

name: Radicchio
description: Tight purple-white heads, distinctly bitter — grilled, or shredded raw.

tcm.note: Bitter greens are cooling and heat-clearing.

ayurveda.note: Tikta rasa is shita and pitta-clearing.

unani.note: In the hindiba family, which is barid-yabis and well documented in Unani as a liver cooler.

name: Yardlong beans
description: Beans that grow half a metre long, cut into lengths and stir-fried.

tcm.note: Jiang dou is neutral and tonifies the spleen and kidney.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light, in the fresh bean group.

unani.note: Thanda, though windy like other beans.

name: Spiny gourd
description: Small spiky monsoon gourd, fried in slices — a short season and a devoted following.

tcm.note: Grouped with the cooling gourds; no Chinese entry.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light, in the karavellaka family.

name: Beet greens
description: The leafy tops of beetroot — cooked like chard, and usually thrown away.

tcm.note: Read with the cooling leafy greens.

ayurveda.note: Shita, in the leafy group.

histamine.note: Grouped with spinach and chard — the same oxalate-rich family SIGHI rates poorly.

name: Radish greens
description: Peppery radish leaves, cooked into saag or stuffed into parathas.

tcm.note: Read with radish, which is cool and descending.

ayurveda.note: Katu and ushna — the leaf is more pungent than the root.

unani.note: Garam-khushk in desi usage; used to cut phlegm.

name: Pumpkin flowers
description: Bright orange blossoms, battered and fried or stuffed and steamed.

tcm.note: Read with pumpkin; the flower is lighter and cooler.

ayurveda.note: Shita and laghu — very light.

name: Garlic scapes
description: Curling flower stems of the garlic plant — mild garlic with a green-bean snap.

tcm.note: The allium group is warm and dispersing.

ayurveda.note: Lashuna is ushna and tikshna.

unani.note: Garam-khushk, if gentler than the bulb.

name: Bitter melon leaves
description: The vine leaves, cooked as greens — even more bitter than the fruit.

tcm.note: Read with bitter gourd, which is firmly cold and heat-clearing.

ayurveda.note: Tikta and shita in a high degree, like the fruit.

unani.note: Barid-yabis; used for the same blood-cooling purposes as karela.

name: Sweet potato leaves
description: The vine tops, stir-fried with garlic — soft, faintly sweet, slightly slippery.

tcm.note: Read with the leafy greens; cooling and moistening.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light.

name: Chinese celery
description: Thin hollow stalks with a far stronger flavour than Western celery.

tcm.note: Qin cai is cool and calms liver yang — long used for high blood pressure.

ayurveda.note: Shita, like celery.

name: King oyster mushroom
description: Thick white stems sliced into rounds — the meatiest of the cultivated mushrooms.

tcm.note: Read with the oyster mushroom group — neutral and mildly tonifying.

ayurveda.note: Mushrooms sit awkwardly in the classical texts.

histamine.note: Low fresh; mushrooms climb quickly as they age.

name: Straw mushroom
description: Small egg-shaped mushrooms, almost always sold tinned — a hotpot and stir-fry regular.

tcm.note: Cao gu is cool and clears summer heat in the Chinese reading.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

histamine.note: Low tinned; raw straw mushrooms are toxic, which is a separate hazard.

name: Pea shoots
description: The young tendrils and leaves of the pea plant, wilted in seconds with garlic.

tcm.note: Read with the tender leafy greens; cooling and light.

ayurveda.note: Shita and laghu.

name: Lotus stem
description: The rhizome, sliced into lace-patterned rounds — crisp when quick-cooked, floury when slow.

tcm.note: Lian ou is cool raw and cools the blood; cooked long it turns tonifying instead.

ayurveda.note: Shita and grahi — binding, used for loose stools.

unani.note: Thanda-tar; a Kashmiri and Punjabi winter vegetable.

name: Turnip greens
description: Peppery leaves from the top of the turnip, cooked long and soft.

tcm.note: Read with the brassica greens.

ayurveda.note: Katu and pungent, like the mustard greens they resemble.

name: Dried okra
description: Whole small okra threaded on strings and sun-dried for winter stews.

tcm.note: Read with okra; drying removes the moistening quality.

ayurveda.note: Shita, though drying makes it ruksha rather than slimy.

unani.note: Thanda-khushk; the dried form loses okra's characteristic wetness.

name: Jerusalem artichoke
description: Knobbly sweet tuber, unrelated to the artichoke — famous for the wind it causes.

tcm.note: A new-world tuber with no classical entry.

ayurveda.note: Read as shita and heavy; strongly vata-provoking.

histamine.note: Low for histamine. Its inulin content is a FODMAP problem, not a histamine one.

name: Samphire
description: Salty coastal succulent, blanched briefly and eaten with fish.

tcm.note: Read with the sea vegetables, which are cold and softening.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry; salty and read as shita.

histamine.note: Low, though it grows in the same salt environment as the sea vegetables.

nutrition.highlight: salty enough to need no seasoning

name: Fiddlehead fern
description: Tightly coiled young fern shoots — a brief hill-country spring vegetable.

tcm.note: Jue cai is cool and heat-clearing in the Chinese record.

ayurveda.note: Regional rather than classical.

histamine.note: Low. They must be cooked thoroughly — raw fiddleheads cause illness, which is a separate matter.

name: Banana stem
description: The inner core of the banana trunk, sliced into rings — watery and faintly bitter.

tcm.note: No Chinese entry; read as cooling and diuretic.

ayurveda.note: Shita and mutrala (diuretic) — a classical food for urinary complaints and stones.

unani.note: Thanda-tar; taken as juice for the same purpose.

name: Tinned tomatoes
description: Tomatoes peeled and packed in their own juice — the base of most Western sauces.

tcm.note: Read with tomato, which is cool and fluid-generating.

ayurveda.note: Sour and ushna, like the fresh fruit.

histamine.note: Fresh tomato is already among the highest fresh foods; concentrating and tinning it lifts it further.

name: Mizuna
description: Feathery mild mustard green, eaten raw in salads or wilted at the last second.

tcm.note: A brassica green; cooling and gently heat-clearing.

ayurveda.note: Shita and light.

name: Tatsoi
description: Dark spoon-shaped leaves growing in a flat rosette — a winter green.

tcm.note: Read with bok choy; cooling and moistening.

ayurveda.note: Shita.

name: Sorrel
description: Sharp lemony leaf that turns khaki the moment it hits heat.

tcm.note: Sour and cooling; clears heat.

ayurveda.note: Shita despite the sour taste, like other sour greens.

histamine.note: Very high in oxalate, and sour — the same family as spinach on this scale.

name: Nettle
description: Stings raw, harmless the second it is cooked — a wild spring green.

tcm.note: Read with the cooling wild greens; used to cool blood.

ayurveda.note: Shita and astringent; long used for bleeding.

name: Salsify
description: Long pale root said to taste faintly of oysters, though it mostly does not.

tcm.note: Not classically listed.

ayurveda.note: No classical entry.

name: Rutabaga
description: A cabbage-turnip cross, dense and slightly sweet — mashed more often than not.

tcm.note: Read with turnip, which is neutral and descending.

ayurveda.note: Shita and windy, like the brassicas.

name: Romanesco
description: Lime-green spiralled cones — a brassica that looks designed rather than grown.

tcm.note: Read with cauliflower and broccoli.

ayurveda.note: Shita, with the brassicas.

name: Cardoon
description: The stalks of an artichoke relative, blanched and braised — bitter and fibrous.

tcm.note: Read with artichoke.

ayurveda.note: Tikta and shita.

name: Chicory root
description: Roasted and ground as a coffee stretcher, or brewed as a bitter liver tea.

tcm.note: Bitter and heat-clearing.

ayurveda.note: Tikta rasa is shita.

unani.note: Kasni is a well-documented Unani liver cooler — barid-yabis.

name: Wasabi
description: Grated green rhizome whose heat vanishes within minutes of grating.

tcm.note: Read with the mustard family — hot and dispersing.

ayurveda.note: Katu and ushna in a high degree.

histamine.note: Low. Most 'wasabi' sold is horseradish with dye, which is a labelling matter.

name: Winged beans
description: Four-ridged pods eaten whole — every part of the plant is edible.

tcm.note: No classical Chinese entry.

ayurveda.note: Shita, in the fresh bean group.

name: Ash plantain
description: A starchy Sri Lankan plantain cooked as a vegetable, never eaten ripe.

tcm.note: Read with plantain.

ayurveda.note: Shita and grahi, like raw banana.

name: Drumstick flower
description: The moringa tree's white blossoms, cooked with dal or scrambled with egg.

tcm.note: Read with the drumstick pod and leaf.

ayurveda.note: Shigru is ushna throughout the plant.

name: Agathi leaves
description: Slightly bitter leaves eaten in Tamil households, traditionally once a month.

tcm.note: No Chinese entry.

ayurveda.note: Tikta and shita; taken as a periodic cleanser.

nutrition.highlight: eaten once a month, by custom

name: Gongura
description: Intensely sour red-stemmed leaves — the defining green of Andhra cooking.

tcm.note: Sour and cooling.

ayurveda.note: Shita, though its sour rasa is ushna by taste.

histamine.note: Very sour, and usually made into a pickle or long-cooked chutney.

name: Ponnanganni
description: Small creeping green cooked as a keerai, long associated with eyesight.

tcm.note: No Chinese entry.

ayurveda.note: Shita; a cooling keerai.

name: Collard greens
description: Big flat brassica leaves cooked long and slow until they give up entirely.

tcm.note: A brassica green; cooling.

ayurveda.note: Shita and windy.

histamine.note: Low, though long-cooked greens held warm are a different matter.

name: Ube
description: Vivid purple yam, used as much for its colour as its mild sweetness.

tcm.note: Read with the yams; neutral and spleen-strengthening.

ayurveda.note: Shita and guru.

name: Taro stem
description: The leaf stalks of colocasia, cooked with sour agents to cut the itch.

tcm.note: Read with taro.

ayurveda.note: Shita and astringent.

histamine.note: Low; the itch is oxalate, which the souring agent neutralises.
